"If <condition>:" is checked once, before the line runs; when it fails the line does nothing. - "The count of numbers instruction j changed" is how many positions held a different value after instruction j than before it — the whole line, all its times over. A line that does nothing (cancelled, failed condition, an undo of nothing, or a "from now on" line) changed 0. - Positions count from 0. "The number at position i of the list" is the value there at the moment the instruction runs; "the starting list" is the list before anything ran; "this instruction's list B" is the private list printed on that line; "its own position" is the position of the number being replaced.

If several lines are waiting on the same k they run in listing order, and anything they in turn release runs right after them in the same way.

"If <condition>:" is checked once, before the line runs; when it fails the line does nothing. "k times over" runs the whole line k times in a row, re-reading every reference each time (the condition is not re-checked).

A line that does nothing (cancelled, failed condition, an undo of nothing, or a "from now on" line) changed 0. "Positions instruction j applied to" are the positions its selection covered when it ran (for a move — a sort, reverse, rotate or swap — every position that received a value from another position, even an equal value, but not a position whose value it left where it was; for an undo: the positions it put back). Any other line that ran applied to its whole selection even where a value came out the same; only a line that was skipped — cancelled, a failed condition, an undo of nothing, a repeat of a cancelled line, or a "from now on" line — applied to no positions. "The same selection as instruction j" applies j's current selection rule to the list now.
- A line's operand is the value it combines with the number being replaced: the 7 in "the number plus 7", the 1 in "1 minus the number", the count in "the number times the count of numbers instruction 3 changed". "As it is currently defined" includes every such change so far. "Apply instruction j's operation (as it is currently defined) to the list now, as one more run of it" runs the whole of line j once more as it is now defined — its selection, its "If" (checked now), its times over and its one-at-a-time order — reading every reference now (nothing, if j is cancelled); "apply the inverse of instruction j's operation" does the same with the operation inverted. Apply the instructions by careful reasoning and report the list after every one; if you are given calculators, use them for arithmetic only. Each instruction says exactly what it does; these are the only rules that live outside the lines.

- Positions count from 0. "The number at position i of the list" is the value there at the moment the instruction runs; "the starting list" is the list before anything ran; "this instruction's list B" is the private list printed on that line; "its own position" is the position of the number being replaced.
- Instructions run in numbered order, each exactly once. A line that says "hold this instruction until instruction k has executed" skips its turn and runs immediately after k. If several lines are waiting on the same k they run in listing order, and anything they in turn release runs right after them in the same way.
- An instruction reads the list as it is right before it runs (one snapshot) and replaces all its selected numbers at once — except a line marked "one number at a time", which updates positions in the stated direction and re-reads the list for each number. "If <condition>:" is checked once, before the line runs; when it fails the line does nothing. "k times over" runs the whole line k times in a row, re-reading every reference each time (the condition is not re-checked).
- "The count of numbers instruction j changed" is how many positions held a different value after instruction j than before it — the whole line, all its times over. A line that does nothing (cancelled, failed condition, an undo of nothing, or a "from now on" line) changed 0. "Positions instruction j applied to" are the positions its selection covered when it ran (for a move — a sort, reverse, rotate or swap — every position that received a value from another position, even an equal value, but not a position whose value it left where it was; for an undo: the positions it put back). Any other line that ran applied to its whole selection even where a value came out the same; only a line that was skipped — cancelled, a failed condition, an undo of nothing, a repeat of a cancelled line, or a "from now on" line — applied to no positions. "The same selection as instruction j" applies j's current selection rule to the list now.
- A line's operand is the value it combines with the number being replaced: the 7 in "the number plus 7", the 1 in "1 minus the number", the count in "the number times the count of numbers instruction 3 changed". An operand given by a "from now on" line is read when the changed line runs, not when the "from now on" line does. "From now on, instruction j ..." changes what j does when its turn comes; such changes stack in the order they run, and a cancelled line stays cancelled. "As it is currently defined" includes every such change so far. "Apply instruction j's operation (as it is currently defined) to the list now, as one more run of it" runs the whole of line j once more as it is now defined — its selection, its "If" (checked now), its times over and its one-at-a-time order — reading every reference now (nothing, if j is cancelled); "apply the inverse of instruction j's operation" does the same with the operation inverted. The inverse of an operation: plus ↔ minus, times ↔ divided exactly, "x minus the number" ↔ itself, whatever x is (a number, a count, a value from a list), reverse ↔ reverse, rotate right by k ↔ rotate left by k, swap ↔ the same swap. "Undo what instruction j actually did" applies the inverse with the exact values j used, at the positions j applied to (for a move: puts the values back the way j moved them), to the list as it is now. A line run k times over is undone run by run, last run first, each with its own values and positions; undoing an undo makes the undone change again, with the same values at the same positions.
- Everything stays an integer; negative numbers are allowed. "Rounded down" is toward minus infinity (−7 divided by 2, rounded down, is −4). "The remainder when a is divided by b" takes the sign of b (the remainder when −7 is divided by 3 is 2). gcd and lcm are never negative; gcd(a, 0) = |a| and lcm(a, 0) = 0. "Divided exactly" always divides without remainder. "Rotate the list right by k" moves every value k positions to the right, wrapping around to the front.

A line that does nothing (cancelled, failed condition, an undo of nothing, or a "from now on" line) changed 0. "Positions instruction j applied to" are the positions its selection covered when it ran (for a move — a sort, reverse, rotate or swap — every position that received a value from another position, even an equal value, but not a position whose value it left where it was; for an undo: the positions it put back). Any other line that ran applied to its whole selection even where a value came out the same; only a line that was skipped — cancelled, a failed condition, an undo of nothing, a repeat of a cancelled line, or a "from now on" line — applied to no positions. "The same selection as instruction j" applies j's current selection rule to the list now.

"Undo what instruction j actually did" applies the inverse with the exact values j used, at the positions j applied to (for a move: puts the values back the way j moved them), to the list as it is now. A line that does nothing (cancelled, failed condition, an undo of nothing, or a "from now on" line) changed 0. "Positions instruction j applied to" are the positions its selection covered when it ran (for a move — a sort, reverse, rotate or swap — every position that received a value from another position, even an equal value, but not a position whose value it left where it was; for an undo: the positions it put back). Any other line that ran applied to its whole selection even where a value came out the same; only a line that was skipped — cancelled, a failed condition, an undo of nothing, a repeat of a cancelled line, or a "from now on" line — applied to no positions. "The same selection as instruction j" applies j's current selection rule to the list now.

"Undo what instruction j actually did" applies the inverse with the exact values j used, at the positions j applied to (for a move: puts the values back the way j moved them), to the list as it is now. A line run k times over is undone run by run, last run first, each with its own values and positions; undoing an undo makes the undone change again, with the same values at the same positions.

"The remainder when a is divided by b" takes the sign of b (the remainder when −7 is divided by 3 is 2). gcd and lcm are never negative; gcd(a, 0) = |a| and lcm(a, 0) = 0.
